# Never Trim a Memory Line Without Checking the Fact Exists Elsewhere

With `MEMORY.md` at 2,496 of its 2,500-character cap on 2026-09-19, a line was selected for compression to make room. The attempt nearly destroyed the only copy of the fact it carried. The resolution was to *move* the line into the Tier A slate file rather than delete it, and additionally to copy the durable fact into the `project-triage` repository so both machines would see it — a repo that uses `master` rather than `main`.

## Key Points

- **Cap pressure creates deletion pressure.** A file four characters from its limit turns every new write into a search for something to remove, and the fastest removal is the one that checks least.
- **A memory line may be the sole copy of its fact.** Trimming for length is a size operation; deleting the only record of a decision is a knowledge operation. Nothing in the editing context distinguishes them.
- **The safe verb is move, not compress.** Relocating the line to the Tier A slate file preserves the content while relieving the index, which is the intended mechanism rather than an emergency measure.
- **Cross-machine durability required a second write.** Tier A memory does not travel between machines, so the durable fact was also copied into `project-triage` — and that repo's default branch is `master`, a detail that breaks any hardcoded `main` assumption.
- **The check is cheap and the loss is silent.** Searching for a second copy costs seconds; the absence of one is discovered only when the fact is needed and gone.

## Details

The near-miss sharpens a rule already implicit in the memory tier's design. Relief at the cap is supposed to come from *migration* — moving a fact from the always-loaded index into a Tier A file that is retrievable but not resident — which is the paired half of writing a Tier A fact at all, as established in [[concepts/memory-cap-relief-by-migration-not-deletion]]. Compression is a tempting third option because it appears to preserve meaning while reclaiming characters, but a compressed line is a lossy rewrite performed under space pressure by an editor whose attention is on the character count, not on what the sentence uniquely records. When the line happens to be the sole surviving statement of a decision, the loss is unrecoverable and undetectable: nothing errors, the file gets shorter, and the fact is simply absent the next time it is needed.

The generalizable discipline is to establish *redundancy before reduction*. Before any trim, the question is whether the content exists in a second location — a project `STATUS.md`, a handoff note, a Tier A file, a commit message — and only if it does is deletion a size decision rather than a knowledge one. This is the same reasoning that made [[concepts/pre-destructive-git-backup-discipline]] insist on a snapshot before a destructive git operation, and the same reasoning behind the 324-row forecast-log catch in [[concepts/cross-machine-conflict-file-triage]], where a resolution rule that looked purely mechanical would have discarded the only copy of real data. The `.errors.log` archive overwrite in [[concepts/error-log-archive-collision-overwrite]] is the case where the check was not made and the content was recovered only because git happened to hold a second copy.

The cross-machine follow-through is the other half of the fix and addresses a different failure mode. Because Tier A memory is machine-local, relocating a fact out of the synced `MEMORY.md` index and into a Tier A slate file makes it *less* visible to the other machine, not more — so a durable fact that both machines need must additionally be written somewhere git replicates. Copying it into `project-triage` achieves that, and the incidental discovery that the repo tracks `master` rather than `main` is exactly the kind of assumption that breaks scripted cross-machine writes. This is the placement reasoning of [[connections/write-the-decision-where-each-consumer-will-look]] applied under a constraint: the relief move and the replication move pull in opposite directions, so both are required.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/memory-cap-relief-by-migration-not-deletion]] — The established mechanism this near-miss reinforces: migrate rather than delete.
- [[connections/always-loaded-context-is-the-expensive-place-to-be-wrong]] — Why the always-loaded index is capped in the first place, and why relief must not cost correctness.
- [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]] — The Tier A/B routing matrix, including the cross-machine constraint invoked here.
- [[concepts/cross-machine-conflict-file-triage]] — A mechanical-looking resolution rule that would have destroyed the only copy of 324 rows.
- [[concepts/error-log-archive-collision-overwrite]] — The case where the second-copy check was skipped and recovery depended on luck.
- [[concepts/pre-destructive-git-backup-discipline]] — Snapshot-before-destruction as the same discipline at the filesystem layer.
- [[connections/write-the-decision-where-each-consumer-will-look]] — Placement reasoning behind the additional `project-triage` copy.

# Concurrent Claude Sessions Working the Same Repos

The 13:10 closeout on 2026-09-19 ran while a second Claude session (started 10:14) was operating on the same repositories. The overlap produced four distinct effects: a suspected reverted edit that turned out to be a bad grep, a handoff-ownership decision, a redundant clone of a repo that was already present under a differently-spelled name, and a real `global-memory` merge conflict from the other session's push.

## Key Points

- **A failed grep is visually identical to a reverted edit.** Checking whether the concurrent session had undone the daily-backup manifest fix returned nothing; the cause was bad quoting in the grep, not a revert. Verification requires reading the file, not trusting a grep's silence.
- **Handoffs are written per session, not per machine.** The other session's handoff did not cover the backup-divergence fix, so a separate handoff was written and the other session's was left untouched.
- **Duplicate work slipped through the name gap.** `DEV/Linda Projects` (with a space) was already in the backup manifest; the concurrent session cloned it again as `Linda_Projects`, leaving two clones of one private repo.
- **Concurrent sessions cause genuine merge conflicts in `global-memory`** — pulling before committing memory should be the expected step, not an exception.
- **A detached HEAD found during the sweep was safe** because the commit was already on `origin/main` — check before treating it as damage.

## Details

Multi-session concurrency on shared repositories converts several ordinarily-reliable signals into ambiguous ones. An unexpected file state now has at least three explanations — this session's own action, the other session's action, or a measurement error — and the default assumption that "nothing changed it but me" no longer holds. The grep incident is the instructive case: the natural reading of an empty result was that the concurrent session had reverted the manifest fix, which is a plausible story that fits the evidence and is wrong. Reading the file directly settled it. This is the same step-down-to-ground-truth move recorded in [[connections/step-down-to-ground-truth-when-the-surface-lies]], with the wrinkle that concurrency supplies a *believable* wrong hypothesis, which is what makes the shortcut tempting.

The handoff decision establishes a scoping rule for a situation the closeout discipline had not previously faced. [[concepts/closeout-scope-discipline-other-sessions-work]] settled that a sweep covers its own session's surface and leaves another session's in-flight work alone; the corollary drawn here is that the same applies to the *documentation* of that work. Editing the other session's handoff to append this session's fix would attribute work across a boundary the reader cannot see, so a separate handoff was written and the existing one left as its author wrote it. The redundant `Linda_Projects` clone is the failure that this scoping cannot prevent: two sessions, each acting reasonably on its own information, produced duplicated work because the repository's canonical name contains a space and the second session normalised it. That is a close relative of the name-mismatch false alarms in [[concepts/dev-sync-false-missing-repos]], and the same space-in-path hazard that broke shell sweeps twice in this session — word splitting silently drops entries, so every path must be quoted.

The `global-memory` conflict is the least surprising and most structural finding: two sessions appending to the same memory repository will collide, and the correct posture is to pull before committing rather than to discover the collision at push time. Transcript-log conflicts of this kind already have an established resolution — union merge, keeping every line from both sides, as three independent instances confirmed in [[concepts/dev-sync-2026-09-22-manifest-and-union-merge]]. This is the intra-machine analogue of the cross-machine push collisions in [[concepts/unattended-cross-machine-push-collisions]]: the other writer is now a sibling process rather than another laptop, but the merge cost and the "check whether someone else already handled this" reflex are identical. Two further sweep-level observations round the session out: background sweeps buffer output and can hang, so a fast local pass over dirty and unpushed files is sufficient for sign-off, and dirty files remaining at closeout were live session logs rather than unsaved work.

# Commit Recency Is Not Work Recency: Sync Commits Mask the Active Project

Choosing which project to work on during the 2026-09-24 evening session started from the obvious signal — the most recent commit across repositories — and that signal was wrong. `CFB_Victory_Model` carried the latest timestamps, but its commits were sync commits produced by automation and cross-machine reconciliation, not authored work. The genuinely newest real work was a 13:20 merge group in KeystoneOS, which was selected instead. The same trap had already been hit five days earlier, on 2026-09-19, when `graphify-out` topped the recency ranking on the strength of an automated daily job and had to be excluded before `DataBase_GPS_Reporting` could be identified as the real pick-up repo. A commit timestamp records when the repository was written to, which is a strictly weaker claim than when a human last worked on it.

## Key Points

- **Automation authors commits.** Nightly backups that commit working trees, sync jobs that push reconciled state, scheduled generation jobs, and merge commits from cross-machine pulls all advance the timestamp without representing any human decision.
- **This inflates exactly the repos with the most machinery around them,** so the repositories with the best automation look the most active — an inversion of the signal's intent. `graphify-out` is generated output with a daily job; `CFB_Victory_Model` is heavily synced.
- **The fix is to classify the commit before ranking it:** read the message and the diff, and ask whether a human authored the change. A *group* of related commits at one time (the 13:20 merge group) reads as a work session; a lone `sync`, backup, or generation commit does not.
- **The same distinction resolves cross-machine conflicts,** where the question is likewise whether a change is authored content or mechanical churn rather than simply which copy is newer.
- **A wrong answer here costs a whole session's direction,** not a single file, because it determines which project gets picked up and which handoff gets read.
- **Generated output still gets committed.** On 2026-09-19 `graphify-out`'s 10 generated-output files were committed rather than left dirty — excluding a repo from the *ranking* is separate from leaving its working tree unclean.

## Details

The underlying error is treating a proxy as the property it stands in for. "Most recently committed" is a genuinely useful heuristic for "most recently worked on" in a repository that only a human writes to, and it degrades exactly in proportion to how much automated writing happens. In this stack the automated write volume is substantial: the nightly backup commits and pushes working trees, `dev-sync` pulls and merges across the Windows and Mac machines, union merges append to shared logs, and a daily job regenerates `graphify-out` — each producing commits whose timestamps are recent and whose content is nobody's work. The most-automated repository therefore floats to the top of a recency ranking, which is precisely backwards from the intent of the query. The `repo-behind-blocked` failure on 9/24 is a reminder of how much of this traffic there is: the backup's ordinary mode of operation is to author commits in repositories the human has not touched.

That the same mistake was made twice within a week, on two different repositories and for two different automation causes, is the argument that the heuristic needs replacing rather than remembering. On 9/19 the tell was known in advance — the session explicitly noted that `graphify-out`'s newer commits came from an automated daily job — and the exclusion still had to be made by hand; on 9/24 the same reasoning had to be re-derived for sync commits. A rule applied manually at each use is a rule that will eventually be skipped, and it will be skipped on the evening when the operator is least inclined to read commit messages.

The remedy is the classify-before-resolving discipline that has repeatedly paid off elsewhere in this system. [[concepts/cross-machine-conflict-file-triage]] collapsed thirty-six flagged conflicts to four by asking what *kind* of difference each one was before adjudicating any of them, and [[connections/newer-is-not-more-complete]] generalizes the lesson that a later timestamp says nothing about content when the two versions are not revisions of one another. Applied to commit history, the classification is between authored and mechanical commits, and the cheap tell is shape rather than content: a cluster of commits within a short window, touching related files, with human-written messages, is a work session; an isolated commit with a generated message is not.

A practical corollary is that automated commits should be made identifiable so this classification is mechanical rather than a judgement call each time. Consistent message prefixes for backup, sync, and generation commits, or a distinct committer identity, would let a recency query filter them out directly — the same reasoning that makes greppable `skipped` markers in [[concepts/decommissioned-leg-verified-by-skipped-markers]] turn a cutover into a checkable line count. Absent such a convention, every "what was I last working on?" question requires reading the commits, and the risk is that the reading is skipped precisely on the evenings when the answer matters most.

# Connection: A Check's Silence Is Not a Negative Result

## The Connection

Three findings from a single day share one shape: a check returned a quiet, reassuring answer, and the quiet came from the check being unable to speak rather than from there being nothing to say. A sync pass reported ~140 repositories clean because it had never contacted the remote. A grep returned nothing because its quoting was wrong, not because the text was absent. And in the third case the inverse held — a check spoke loudly (`PUSH ERR`) about a message that meant success — which completes the picture: the mapping between what a check emits and what is true had come apart in both directions on the same morning.

## Key Insight

**A negative result carries information only if the check was capable of producing a positive one.** That capability is a separate fact from the result, it is almost never printed alongside the result, and it is exactly what an operator skips verifying when the result is the one they hoped for. `git status` cannot report "behind" without a prior fetch; a badly-quoted grep cannot match anything; neither announces its own incapacity. In both cases the output is indistinguishable from the healthy case — which is what makes the failure mode chronic rather than occasional.

The direction of the bias is what makes this class expensive. A check that has been silently disabled fails *toward reassurance*: 140 clean repos and an empty grep both look like good news, so nothing prompts a second look. Compare the opposite bias in [[concepts/dev-sync-false-missing-repos]], where the same skill's flags overstated the problem — those findings were investigated precisely because they were alarming, and they all evaporated. The alarming wrong answer gets audited; the reassuring wrong answer gets believed. A tool that can be wrong in both directions is a work queue rather than a report, and its *clean* verdicts need scrutiny at least as much as its flags do.

The practical rule that falls out is to make capability part of the output rather than part of the operator's memory. A sync report should carry fetch evidence or decline to claim cleanliness; a grep used as a decision input should be validated against a string known to be present before its absence is trusted; a push classifier should key on the exit code, which is the field that actually encodes success, rather than on the presence of text. In each case the fix moves the assurance from "I remembered to do the enabling step" into the artifact itself — the same move as [[connections/durable-log-is-the-contract-for-scheduled-work]], and the same reason [[concepts/clear-the-error-log-only-after-a-clean-run]] gates a state change on a verified re-run rather than on an intended fix.

## Evidence

- 2026-09-19, sync: the first inventory pass "reported repos 'clean' without ever running `git fetch`, so the claim was based only on local state." Re-running with fetch revealed five repos behind. Recorded as "the single biggest failure mode of this skill."
- 2026-09-19, closeout: checking whether the concurrent session had reverted the daily-backup manifest fix returned nothing; "a bad grep quoting was the false alarm." Stated lesson: "A failed grep can look exactly like a reverted edit. Verify by reading the file, not by grep alone."
- 2026-09-19, backup: the `repo-push:dotclaude` hook failure resolved to the log line `PUSH ERR | Everything up-to-date` — git's success output for a no-op push, classified as an error. The inverse defect: a check speaking where it should be silent.
- Same day, same hazard class: "Shell sweeps break on repo paths with spaces — word splitting silently drops entries." A sweep that drops an entry reports clean on the entries it kept.
- Counterpoint, 2026-09-11 ([[concepts/dev-sync-false-missing-repos]]): the same skill's *positive* flags — four "not a repo" folders, five "missing" repos, two `repo-diverged` errors — all evaporated on inspection, because alarming results get audited.
